fact: Marmeladov, a drunken former civil servant, tells Raskolnikov in a tavern that his daughter Sonya has been forced into prostitution to feed the family.
Marmeladov is fatally trampled by a carriage in the street; Raskolnikov gives his last money to the family to pay for the funeral.
Raskolnikov's mother Pulcheria Alexandrovna writes describing Dunya's engagement to Luzhin and her earlier ordeal with Svidrigailov, her former employer.
Svidrigailov tells Raskolnikov that the ghost of his dead wife, Marfa Petrovna, has visited him three times since her burial.
The examining magistrate Porfiry Petrovich conducts a psychological cat-and-mouse interrogation of Raskolnikov, implying suspicion without ever directly accusing him.
Luzhin secretly plants a 100-rouble note in Sonya's pocket at the Marmeladov memorial dinner, then publicly accuses her of theft, as revenge on Raskolnikov for turning the family against him.
Svidrigailov reveals that he overheard Raskolnikov's confession to Sonya through the wall of the adjoining room, since he has been renting the room next door.
Svidrigailov offers Dunya 10,000 roubles to break off her engagement to Luzhin; enraged, she refuses and orders him out.
Svidrigailov gives Sonya 3,000 roubles before his death, funding her eventual journey to Siberia with Raskolnikov.
Svidrigailov commits suicide by shooting himself, after a night of disturbing dreams, in a public place shortly before dawn.

fact: Raskolnikov confesses to the murders at the police station after first going to Sonya and kissing the ground at the Hay Market crossroads, per her earlier instruction.

fact: Raskolnikov is sentenced to eight years of penal servitude in Siberia; Sonya follows him there.

In the Epilogue, Raskolnikov has a fever dream about a plague of self-righteous ideological "trichinae" that turns people against each other, shortly before his spiritual turn toward Sonya and the Gospels.
